tagline.text: A 25 m waterfall in a Biliran valley that drifts down as fine mist

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–May, the relatively less rainy period (avoid right after rain)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–700 (day trip from Naval, incl. motorcycle taxi, entrance fee, guide and snacks, per person)

children.text: Ulan-Ulan Falls is a waterfall about 25 m high in a valley in Barangay Sampao, Almeria, on Biliran Island, famous for spray that drifts down like rain. It is about 30 minutes by motorcycle from the provincial capital Naval, and you reach it by walking down a forest path from the registration post at the entrance.

Ulan-Ulan Falls lies in Barangay Sampao in the municipality of Almeria, in the northwest of Biliran Island. From the provincial capital Naval, you take the national highway, turn off toward Sabang or Jamorawn, and continue through Tamarindo into Sampao; by car or motorcycle the trip is said to take
20–30 minutes

. One map in the OpenStreetMap family places it at around latitude 11.6282, longitude 124.4384. That value was confirmed on only one map source, so use Google Maps together with local directions when navigating. Biliran became a separate province in 1992 after splitting from Leyte, and locals count nearly thirty waterfalls on the island. Ulan-Ulan is the easiest to reach and relatively well maintained, so it is the one most often recommended to first-time visitors. It is not a large tourist complex but a modest attraction managed by villagers, so please visit respectfully, remembering that the entrance and guide fees are income for the village. Because Biliran is reached overland from Tacloban, the journey can easily eat up a day, so plan at least one night and put the falls in a morning slot.
Ulan means "rain" in the local language. The falls drop from a height of about

(sources say 20–25 m) through a cleft in the rock, and the fine mist rising at the bottom drifts about like rain. The water falls in a single line like a horse's tail and sometimes spreads into a fan shape depending on the flow. Behind the falls you can see the ridge of Mt. Panamao, which rises above 1,000 m, and the road to the entrance passes the rice fields of Sampao.
At the entrance there is a visitor registration post where you write your name, address and contact details and pay the fee. The entrance fee is

per person according to recent sources, and parking is free. Next to the post there is a restroom and a small stall selling snacks and drinks. There are no cottages or restaurants, and guides note that mobile signal is weak in this area.
You walk down to the falls from the registration post. Recent guides describe concrete steps with handrails that take
15–20 minutes
, while many older blog posts report that muddy ground and slippery rocks made the walk take
about 30 minutes

. Trail conditions change from year to year, and some visitors report landslide damage, so treat the times in this guide as a rough reference. The pool below the falls is very cold and the current in the middle is strong, so it is safer to dip your feet at the edge and enjoy the spray rather than swim.

blocks.title: A 25 m waterfall that falls like drizzle

children.text: Water dropping in a single fall breaks up and sends drops flying out in front of the falls. This is where the name comes from, and standing close feels like being rained on without an umbrella.

When the flow is low it falls as a thin stream, and when it is high it spreads wide. The same falls can look quite different depending on the season, so comparing the day after rain with a clear day is part of the fun.

blocks.title: Cold water and the pool edge

children.text: The water is described as cool, at about
. Many guides say the current in the middle is strong, so sitting on the rocks at the edge is the sensible way to relax.
The large rocks around the pool are good for eating snacks and taking photos. The stall is only near the entrance, so bring water and snacks before you head down.
A smaller waterfall said to be about
5–10 minutes

on foot upstream of Ulan-Ulan Falls, with a large pool that is reported to be good for swimming. Some visitors could not reach it because the trail was damaged, and others found it hard because of a stream crossing, so check the conditions before you decide.

Terraced rice fields and mountain ridges line the way to the entrance, so the ride itself is worth seeing. If you take a motorcycle taxi, you can ask the driver to stop for a moment so you can take photos.

blocks.title: A distance that suits a day trip

children.text: It is close to Naval, so you can visit in the morning and plan something else for the afternoon. ASEMCO Hilltop Resort and Erika's Nature Park are nearby in the same direction, so they can be combined in one outing.

items.title: Half-day course from Naval
items.subtitle: From the registration post to the falls

children.text: Find a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) in central Naval and set out for Sampao. Tell the driver clearly that you want to be dropped at the Ulan-Ulan Falls entrance, and agree in advance on the fare and whether he will wait for the return trip.
Arrive at the registration post, write your name and contact details, and pay the
entrance fee. Hire a local guide if you want one, and keep water and a change of clothes with you.
Walk down the steps and forest path to the falls. Recent guides say
15–20 minutes
, but it can take longer after rain.
Rest and take photos on the rocks in front of the falls, feeling the spray. The current in the middle of the pool is strong, so get into the water only at the edge.
Decide about Recoletos Falls upstream after checking the trail condition. If it looks too difficult, skip it and leave plenty of time for the climb back up.
Climb back up to the registration post, ride the motorcycle taxi back to Naval and have lunch.
The forest path is dangerous after dark, so plan to be back at the entrance by
at the latest. Check the latest opening status and hours locally just before your visit.
Cebu Pacific and Philippine Airlines fly direct from Manila (NAIA) to Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport (TAC) in Tacloban. Schedules and fares vary by season, so check the airline app.
From Tacloban Airport you can take a jeepney to the city van terminal, and one report mentions about
. Many reviews say airport taxis are expensive.
Biliran Island has no airport, and some reports say Grab is hard to use in this area.
Vans to Naval run from the Tacloban van terminal. Reports put the fare at about
and the trip at about
2.5–3 hours
. If there is no van to Naval, another option described is to take a van toward Ormoc and change at Lemon Crossing.
If you are coming from Cebu, you can take a fast craft to Ormoc and change to a Naval-bound van at the Ormoc van terminal. Schedules and fares can change, so confirm them at the terminal.

items.title: From Naval to the falls entrance

children.text: A motorcycle taxi from Naval to Sampao takes about
25–30 minutes
. One-way fares differ between reviews and blogs at
, and one guide gives about
for a round trip including waiting time.
If you go by car or a rented motorcycle, use Google Maps to find Sampao from Naval or Almeria. One guide gives a motorcycle rental of at least
per day, with fuel extra.
On rainy days the road is slippery, so ask the driver to slow down.

Biliran has no distinct dry season and rain falls throughout the year, so catching a clear day matters most. March to May is generally the relatively less rainy period, and guides say the falls can be crowded then.

Right after rain the flow grows and the falls look more impressive, but the path becomes very slippery and the current in the pool is strong. Guides advise against visiting in bad weather, so check the weather forecast and any typhoon information before you set out.

There are few places to stay near the falls, so most people stay in central Naval and make a day trip. Naval has hotels and inns, and there are places in the same direction such as ASEMCO Hilltop Resort, so choose to suit your schedule and budget. Room rates and availability are best confirmed locally.

It is safest to eat in Naval, at a restaurant or your lodging. At the falls entrance there is only a stall selling snacks and drinks, with no restaurant or cottage, so have lunch in Naval and bring water and snacks. For local restaurants, long-established places with clear signs and price lists rarely disappoint.

Naval has a long-running market and small eateries where you can try simple food such as grilled fish, noodles and local snacks. After the falls, a hot meal in town after changing out of wet clothes is a sensible plan. Change money and withdraw cash in Naval beforehand, and carry plenty of small bills near the falls.
Mobile signal is weak, so save maps and contact numbers beforehand and stay with a guide or companions.
The forest path and rocks are slippery, so wear shoes with firm soles or sandals with straps. Flip-flops are not recommended.
The water is cold, so bring a change of clothes, a towel and a waterproof bag. The spray is heavy and can soak cameras and phones.
Be sure to write your name and contact details at the registration post, and tell the motorcycle driver when you will come back.
If you agree the waiting fee for the round trip in advance, you do not have to worry about finding a ride back.
Carry your trash out, and do not leave food behind anywhere except at the stall.
Hours are not given in the sources, so plan to arrive early in the morning and check the latest announcements.
If you want to go to Recoletos Falls upstream, ask at the registration post or your guide about the trail condition first.
Entrance and motorcycle fares are small amounts, so carry plenty of 20, 50 and 100 peso bills. Change can be hard to come by near the falls.
The forest path to the falls is very slippery in rain and some visitors report landslide damage, so do not go in bad weather.
Guides say the current in the middle of the pool is strong, so get in the water only at the edge and never swim alone.
Avoid visiting alone or climbing the path after dark. Be back at the entrance before sunset.
An older report mentions getting lost because of the lack of signs. At forks, check the way with your guide or the registration post staff.
Reviews say the path to Recoletos Falls upstream requires crossing a stream and is very hard, so do not push yourself.
Fees and fares differ between sources, and the sources range from 2016 to 2026. Confirm current prices locally.
